title: The Road to Jerusalem, and Civilis on the Rhine
sum: Book 5 opens with Titus marching an army up to Jerusalem. Before he tells of the siege, Tacitus stops to explain who the Jews are. He gives five stories of their origin, prefers the one about an Egyptian plague and an exile led by Moyses, runs through their customs with open dislike, describes their land and the Dead Sea, and sketches their history from Pompey to the governor Felix. Then he describes the city, its three quarreling commanders and the omens before the siege (5:1-13).

At 5:14 the book turns to the Rhine, where the Batavian leader Civilis and the Roman general Cerialis fight over marsh, dam and river until Civilis asks for a talk. The text breaks off in the middle of his speech at 5:26. Tacitus's own account of the fall of Jerusalem is lost, so Josephus is the main surviving witness to it.
readings: Read as a Roman's report on a foreign people

Tacitus writes for Romans, in the usual form of an ethnography: origin, customs, land, history (as Bloch lays out in his study of the passage, reviewed by van der Horst). He reports what Greek and Egyptian writers said and adds his own verdicts. The Jews are an odd, stubborn people whose defeat he is about to tell.

Almost every custom he lists has a Bible root: circumcision (Genesis 17), the Sabbath and the seventh year (Exodus 20; Leviticus 25), no pork (Leviticus 11), unleavened bread (Exodus 12), one God with no image (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 6:4), Sodom's fire (Genesis 19). Tacitus gets the practices mostly right and the reasons wrong, because he takes his reasons from Egyptian stories, not from the Law.
Read as the setting of Jesus' warning

The war Tacitus is about to tell is the one Jesus described: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). Tacitus has the army, the camp "not far from Jerusalem" and the earthworks; the Gospels have the warning given a generation earlier.

views.C: A Christian who takes the Bible as true reads Tacitus as an outsider's testimony. On practices he is a useful witness: the Jews of his day kept circumcision, the Sabbath, a pork ban, burial, one God and no images, just as the Law commands (Genesis 17:11; Exodus 20:4, 20:8-11; Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 6:4). On origins he is wrong, and the Bible's account of Abraham, Moses and the Exodus answers him. Later he says plainly that the Jews put up no statues and that the sanctuary held no image (5:5, 5:9), which agrees with Exodus 20:4. He reports the omens and the oracle of a ruler from Judea, and gives them to Vespasian and Titus (5:13). A Christian reads the oracle as the Bible's promise of a ruler for all peoples (Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17; Daniel 7:13-14) and finds that ruler in Jesus (Matthew 2:2; Luke 1:32-33). Whether Jesus' warning in Luke 21 looks only to AD 70 or also beyond it is a Christian dispute (see the topic on the Olivet discourse).
views.H: Historians ask where Tacitus got this. He says "most writers agree" and names no one (5:3). Josephus names the Egyptian writers Manetho and Lysimachus as the source of the leper-exile story (Against Apion 1.14-35). Bloch, in a study of the passage reviewed by Pieter van der Horst, finds that Tacitus mostly follows what earlier writers had said about the Jews, even where they contradict each other, that he paints the picture with a broad brush for the story it leads into, and that part of its purpose is to show the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and lose their temple. Tacitus differs from Josephus on points where Josephus was closer to events: he calls John of Gischala "Bargioras" (5:12) and says Varus punished the rebel Simon where Josephus has Gratus (5:9). On Pompey's sanctuary the two can both be right: Josephus lists gold furniture Pompey saw (Jewish War 1.7.6) but says the inmost room held "nothing at all" (5.5.5), and Cassius Dio, too, says the Jews never had a statue of their god even in Jerusalem (Roman History 37.17). The Histories were written about AD 100-110, decades after the events (Wikipedia, 'Histories (Tacitus)').
views.R: For Tacitus's readers a legion, a procurator or a Roman Knight needed no explaining. His "us" is Roman: Pompey conquered the Jews, Claudius handed the province to freedmen, "it made us angrier" that the Jews alone held out (5:9-10). Romans tolerated many gods and were suspicious of a people who would worship none but their own and refused statues even of the emperor (5:5). He treats the omens the way Romans did, as warnings the Jews should have averted with sacrifice and vows (5:13). Book 5 also shows the shape of Rome's empire: a Jewish war and a Rhine war ending in the same year, with the same new dynasty watching both.
views.J: Josephus tells the same war from inside: Titus's army (Jewish War 5.1.6), the three factions (5.1), John's trick at the feast of unleavened bread (5.3.1), the omens (6.5.3) and the oracle of a world ruler (6.5.4). Where Tacitus says the Jews worshiped a wild ass, Josephus answers that Pompey, Crassus and Titus found nothing of the sort (Against Apion 2.7). Acts has Felix and Drusilla (Acts 24), Agrippa and Bernice (Acts 25-26), the Roman barracks next to the temple (Acts 21:31-37) and the false prophet "the Egyptian" (Acts 21:38). The Gospels give Jesus' warnings (Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 24:1-2). Philo and Josephus both tell of Caligula's statue (5:9).

deep.h: Five origins, and what the Bible says
deep.b:
Tacitus's five origin stories (5:2) and his preferred sixth (5:3) are best read next to Genesis and Exodus.

  • Crete and Mount Ida. A pun, Idaei into Judaei. The Bible gives the name: Judah, Jacob's son (Genesis 29:35).
  • Egypt under Isis, led by Hierosolymus and Judas. Judas is Judah; Hierosolymus is an invented founder from the Greek name of Jerusalem.
  • Ethiopians under Cepheus. Ethiopia is the Bible's Cush. Moses had married a Cushite woman (Numbers 12:1), and Josephus tells the story of his Ethiopian campaign (Antiquities 2.10.2). Claude's guess is a distorted echo, nothing more.
  • Assyrians who took part of Egypt. The closest outline to Genesis: a people from the east who went through Egypt and settled in the Hebrew country (Genesis 11:31; Genesis 14:13; Genesis 12:10).
  • Solymi of Homer. The Bible's early name for the city is Salem (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2), and Josephus says some tied it to Homer's Solyma (Antiquities 7.3.2).
  • Moyses and the Egyptian plague (5:3). The thirst, the rock and the plentiful water echo Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11; the rest reverses Exodus. In Exodus the plagues fall on Egypt (Exodus 7-12) and the people leave at the king's own urging (Exodus 12:31-33).
deep.refs: Genesis 29:35; Genesis 14:13; Numbers 12:1; Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11; Exodus 12:31-33

deep.h: What a Roman got right, and what he got wrong
deep.b:
Right, or close: circumcision as a mark (Genesis 17:11); the Sabbath on the seventh day (Exodus 20:8-11); the seventh year of rest (Leviticus 25:4); no pork (Leviticus 11:7); unleavened bread tied to a hurried departure (Exodus 12:34, 39; Deuteronomy 16:3); one God known by the mind with no image (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 20:4); every child raised (Josephus, Against Apion 2.25); burial of the dead (Genesis 23:19-20); the fire on the plain (Genesis 19:24); the city's temple with only priests at its inner rooms, and an inmost room with no image in it (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.5); the Jews' keeping apart from outsiders (Acts 10:28).

Wrong, or one-sided: the origin of the people; Moses as an Egyptian exile; the animal image in the shrine (the Bible's best-known animal images in Israel, Aaron's calf and Jeroboam's calves, are sins, Exodus 32:4; 1 Kings 12:28-29, and the cherubim over the ark are commanded sculptures that show no god, Exodus 25:18-20); the Sabbath as laziness (Mark 2:27); lust and hatred of outsiders (the Law commands love of the foreigner); the idea that Moses invented the laws to bind a refugee crowd (Exodus 20); the identification of John as Bargioras. And almost every reason given for a custom is Tacitus's or his sources', not the Law's.
deep.refs: Genesis 17:11; Exodus 20:8-11; Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 6:4; Acts 10:28; Mark 2:27; Exodus 32:4; 1 Kings 12:28-29; Exodus 25:18-20

deep.h: Tacitus and Josephus side by side
deep.b:
The two writers cover the same last year of Jerusalem from different sides.

  • Army: both name the 5th, 10th, 15th and 12th legions (5:1; Jewish War 5.1.6). Josephus counts 2,000 men from Alexandria and 3,000 from the Euphrates guards; Tacitus names legions.
  • Factions: three leaders in both, and John's trick at the temple in both (5:12; Jewish War 5.1-5.3). Josephus names the feast; Tacitus does not. The name Bargioras goes to different men.
  • Omens: fiery armies in the sky, a gate that opens, a voice about leaving (5:13; Jewish War 6.5.3). Josephus puts them before the war and says the learned read them as warnings; Tacitus says the crowd would not turn.
  • Oracle: a ruler from Judea. Both give it to the Flavians (5:13; Jewish War 6.5.4).
  • Numbers: Tacitus has 600,000 in the city, "we have been told"; Josephus has 600,000 of the poor dead carried out the gates, as eminent citizens who ran to Titus told him, and 1,100,000 dead in the whole siege (Jewish War 5.13.7; 6.9.3).
  • Attitude: Tacitus is a Roman outsider who calls the Jews superstitious; Josephus is a Jewish insider who calls the rebel leaders tyrants and says men "perish by those miseries which they madly and voluntarily bring upon themselves" (6.5.3).

deep.h: Felix and Drusilla, Agrippa and Bernice
deep.b: Two of the people in Tacitus's list are people of Acts. Felix (5:9) is the governor before whom Paul pleaded (Acts 23:24; Acts 24:10): same office, name and period; Josephus calls him the brother of Pallas (Antiquities 20.7.1), Tacitus's Annals agree (12.54), Suetonius lists him among Claudius's freedmen, says Claudius made him governor, and says he became "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28). The Felix of Acts is afraid, greedy and unjust (Acts 24:25-27), which agrees with Tacitus's "king's power with a slave's mind". Drusilla: Tacitus's is Cleopatra's granddaughter; Acts' is "a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24), whom Josephus says was Agrippa II's sister and left her husband Azizus to marry Felix (Antiquities 20.7.2). The three accounts fit best if Felix had two wives called Drusilla, as the editor of the Suetonius translation holds (footnote 537). Whiston, in his notes, also has Felix marry a granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra, but thinks Tacitus mixed her up with the Jewish Drusilla. Agrippa (5:1) is the king of Acts 25-26, and Bernice his sister. Verdicts: Felix very likely; Agrippa very likely; the royal Drusilla and the Jewish Drusilla probably two women.

deep.title: The Exodus told backward
deep.b: My reading: Tacitus's account of Moyses keeps nearly every beat of Exodus and Numbers and turns each one around. In Exodus the plagues fall on Egypt; in Tacitus the disease is among the exiles. In Exodus God sends Moses (Exodus 3:10); in Tacitus the exiles pick a leader who first rescues them. God gives water at a command (Exodus 17:6); wild asses show where it is. God gives the laws at Sinai (Exodus 20); Moyses makes them to be different. Even Egypt's gods return: Hammon, Apis and the sacred animal. It looks like the Exodus as Egyptian priests and their Greek hearers might have remembered it, with Egypt as the injured party. Josephus saw the same shape in Manetho's Osarsiph story, where the laws are "mainly opposite to the customs of the Egyptians" (Against Apion 1.26).
deep.refs: Exodus 3:10; Exodus 7-12; Exodus 17:6; Exodus 20; Against Apion 1.26

deep.title: Why the Jewish excursus comes just before the siege
deep.b: My reading: placing the Jewish origins, customs and omens directly before the siege makes the siege read as the end of a people who were strange from the start. The Dead Sea, the burned plain, the "vilest of nations" and the omens they would not heed all lead toward the same ending. Bloch argues that part of the excursus's purpose is to show that the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and to lose their only temple (reviewed by van der Horst). The Christian reader has a different frame: Jesus wept over the city (Luke 19:41) and foretold its fall for "you did not recognize the season when you were visited" (Luke 19:44).

echoes: Genesis 17:9-14; Genesis 19:24-28; Exodus 12:34-39; Exodus 17:1-7; Exodus 20:4-11; Leviticus 11:7; Leviticus 25:1-7; Numbers 20:8-11; Numbers 24:17; Deuteronomy 6:4; Daniel 7:13-14; Matthew 24:1-2; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24; Acts 21:31-38; Acts 23:24; Acts 24:24-27; Acts 25:13; Acts 26:2-3; John 11:47-48; Exodus 8:26; Genesis 46:34; Acts 7:22; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Deuteronomy 29:23; 1 Kings 12:28-29; 2 Kings 18:4

settings.to: educated Roman readers of the Histories
settings.when: as Titus's army camps before Jerusalem in the year 70
settings.why: To explain the people and the city Rome is about to attack: where they came from, what they do, what land they hold and how they came under Rome. It also frames the siege as the end of a people Tacitus finds strange and hostile.
settings.readers: Educated Romans in the years around AD 100-110, when the Histories were written (Wikipedia, 'Histories (Tacitus)'). The text shows who they were: Tacitus says "our civil war", "it made us angrier" and treats legions, procurators and Roman Knights as familiar. Bloch's study places the passage within the Greek and Roman tradition of ethnography: origin, customs, land and history (reviewed by van der Horst).
views: Some read the excursus as the usual ethnographic aside, hostile because Romans were hostile to foreign cults.
Bloch argues the passage is built so that even neutral features, such as one-God worship, take on a non-positive color, and that it serves to show the Jews deserved defeat.

settings.what: The oracle of Hammon and the king's order
settings.by: the oracle of Hammon, as Tacitus reports it
settings.why: Inside the story, the god tells the king to purify the kingdom by sending the diseased people away, so that the land will be healed. The tale gives an Egyptian reason for the Exodus: expulsion, not rescue.
settings.readers: Tacitus's Roman readers, who knew this story from Greek and Egyptian writers. Josephus names Manetho and Lysimachus as sources of the plague-and-exile tale and answers them (Against Apion 1.14-35), which shows the story circulated in the Greek world.

settings.to: the exiles, sitting numb and in tears in the empty country
settings.when: after they were rounded up and left in the wilderness
settings.why: Inside the story, to get the crowd moving: gods and men have deserted them, so they should trust themselves and follow whoever first rescues them. It makes Moses a practical organizer, not a man sent by God.
settings.readers: Roman readers meeting the founder of the Jews in a form close to the Egyptian-priest tradition (compare Strabo, who also calls Moses an Egyptian priest and reports his teaching without hostility, Geography 16.2.35). A Christian reader sets it beside Exodus 3-4, where God sends Moses.
views: The speech paints the Jewish founder as a man who invents a religion to bind a refugee crowd.
In Exodus God calls Moses at the burning bush and the people believe when they see the signs (Exodus 3:10; Exodus 4:30-31).

settings.by: a voice "louder than any human voice", heard in the temple
settings.when: before the siege, after the doors of the shrine opened
settings.why: To announce that the gods were leaving, which a Roman would read as the city's protection ending. Josephus has the priests hear "Let us remove hence" at Pentecost (Jewish War 6.5.3).
settings.readers: Roman readers used to omens (see the topic on Roman omens); the Jewish source Josephus gives it to the temple priests.

settings.what: The priests' ancient writings about a ruler from Judea
settings.by: the priests' ancient writings, as Tacitus describes them
settings.to: the people of Judea, especially the besieged
settings.when: cited as the reason most of them held out
settings.why: Most Jews were convinced the writings meant their own nation would rule the world. Tacitus says the riddles pointed to Vespasian and Titus. It explains why the rebels would not yield, and shows how an ambiguous promise gets claimed by whoever wins.
settings.readers: Roman readers, for whom the Flavian victory was proof. Josephus gives the same reading (Jewish War 6.5.4) and Suetonius reports the belief (Vespasian 4). Christians read the promise as fulfilled in Jesus.
views: The ruler is Vespasian (Tacitus; Josephus; Suetonius).
The Jewish nation itself would rule (as Tacitus and Suetonius say).

settings.to: cavalry, auxiliaries, the 14th, the 6th, the 2nd and the army of Germany, one unit at a time
settings.when: the morning of the second battle
settings.why: To raise their pride and shame before the fight: the old glory of Rome, the punishment of a beaten enemy, a nickname for the 14th, a reminder that the 6th made Galba emperor, the promise that the 2nd would dedicate a new eagle, and a plea to the army of Germany to win back its river bank.
settings.readers: Roman readers of military history, for whom the general's address was a set piece. Tacitus says these were not one speech but short talks given as Cerialis rode up to each unit.

settings.when: before the battle in the marsh
settings.why: To make the place itself a witness: they stand where legions died, the marshes help them and the gods of Germany are in sight. He tells them the earlier battle among the Treveri was lost only because they stopped to loot.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who heard in it an enemy general's appeal to place, gods and family.

settings.to: the Batavians, Civilis, and Veleda with her relatives
settings.when: days after the flood and the failed Roman camp
settings.why: To split the rebels: peace for the Batavians, pardon for Civilis, and a chance for Veleda to change the course of the war by one well-timed service to Rome. He warns that exile makes a burden of Civilis and that further harm will bring vengeance and the gods on the rebels.
settings.readers: Roman readers. Tacitus presents Cerialis as lucky and quick but careless about discipline (5:21).

settings.by: the common people and then the nobles of the Batavians
settings.when: as the tribes across the Rhine waver
settings.why: The common people argue that one nation cannot resist the whole world, that the Batavians pay no tribute but give men, and that Roman emperors are better masters than the women of the Germans. The nobles blame Civilis's rage and the gods' anger. The aim of both is to end the war by giving up Civilis.
settings.readers: Roman readers. A Christian reader may compare John 11:48, where a council reasons the same way about Rome.

settings.what: Civilis's speech at the broken bridge
settings.to: Cerialis, who stands on the other broken end
settings.when: at the talk Civilis asked for, over the river Nabalia
settings.why: To defend himself: to a legate of Vitellius he would owe no apology, but toward Vespasian he had long respect, and Primus Antonius, Hordeonius Flaccus and others had urged him to arms. The text breaks off in the middle of his list of those who took arms for Vespasian.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who would weigh the claim against the Batavians' own view in 5:25.

traditions.q: Does the Sabbath commandment still bind Christians, and on which day?
views: The seventh day no longer binds: the Catechism says Sunday "is expressly distinguished from the sabbath" and "for Christians its ceremonial observance replaces that of the sabbath" (Catechism 2175), and that the sabbath "has been replaced by Sunday" (Catechism 2190).

Luther's Large Catechism says the commandment, "according to its gross sense, does not concern us Christians", since it is an outward ordinance of the Old Testament made free through Christ; yet one day a week is set apart for rest and for hearing God's word, and "in itself no one day is better than another" (Large Catechism, Third Commandment).

One day in seven still binds, but the day changed. The Westminster Confession says God "hath particularly appointed one day in seven, for a Sabbath, to be kept holy unto him", which "from the resurrection of Christ, was changed into the first day of the week" (Westminster Confession 21.7).

Yes, the seventh day: the Creator "instituted the Sabbath for all people as a memorial of Creation," and the fourth commandment "requires the observance of this seventh-day Sabbath" (Fundamental Belief 20).

traditions.q: May images be set up in Christian worship and honored?
views: Yes: honor paid to a sacred image is "respectful veneration," not the adoration due to God alone, and "whoever venerates an image venerates the person portrayed in it" (Catechism 2132).

Yes: the Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, 787), which the Orthodox Church receives, says of the holy images "we honour and salute and reverently venerate" them, naming "the image of the incarnation of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ" and that of the Mother of God, and also the angels, apostles, prophets and martyrs (Second Council of Nicaea, in the New Advent English).

Images may stand: in 1525 Luther wrote against those who smashed images, "But images for memorial and witness, such as crucifixes and images of saints, are to be tolerated" (Against the Heavenly Prophets, Luther's Works 40:91, as quoted by lutheranreformation.org).

No images of God, and none taught in churches: God "neither can, nor may be represented by any means," and images may not be tolerated in churches as books for the laity, for God wants his people taught "by the lively preaching of his word" (Heidelberg Catechism 96-98).
